title: The Washington Post — Memo on the Use of Confidential Sources (February 2004)

extracted.subtask_description: Deciding whether information from a confidential source is sufficiently corroborated, described, and attributed to run, and whether the story's sourcing language is literally true to how the information was actually obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum two independent confidential sources for factual information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post prefers at least two sources for factual information that depends on confidential informants, and those sources should be independent of each other. Sources with first-hand or direct knowledge are preferred. A relevant document can sometimes serve as a second source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-source exception requires senior-editor deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are situations where information from a single source will be published, but only after deliberations involving the executive editor, the managing editor, or the appropriate assistant managing editor (AME). The judgment to rely on one source depends on the source's reliability and the basis for the source's information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe sources concretely enough for readers to judge credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post must tell readers as much as possible about why an unnamed source deserves confidence — avoiding bare "sources" or "informed sources" in favor of concrete descriptions (e.g., "sources familiar with the thinking of defense lawyers in the case," "sources on the governor's staff who disagree with his policy"). When sources refuse identification, the story should show that an attempt was made and explain why it failed (e.g., "spoke only on condition that he or she not be named" rather than merely "asked not to be identified" — asking alone is not sufficient grounds for anonymity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rare cases where no useful descriptive information about a source can be given, approval from the relevant AME, managing editor, or executive editor is required before printing information from a totally unidentified source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spokespersons should be on the record for briefings
rubrics_metrics.description: Spokespersons, by virtue of their role, should be on the record for briefings; if they decline to be quoted by name in that context, the Post should protest, seek a publishable explanation, and tell readers what happened if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution language must be literally true
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story refers to "sources" (plural), there must genuinely be multiple sources; if the story says someone "declined to comment," that must be literally true. The Post will not misrepresent that a source "refused to talk" as a way of protecting that source's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any risk that a formulation might mislead the reader about the sourcing must be discussed with an editor before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute facts not produced by the paper's own reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and quotations in a story that were not produced by the Post's own reporting must be attributed, so readers can distinguish between what the reporter directly witnessed and what came from other sources (wire services, pool reporters, email, websites, etc.). If a reporter was not present at a described scene, the story must make that clear; a narrative describing events as recounted by witnesses must include attribution for that reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective/summary attribution (e.g., "This account is drawn from interviews with 19 Somalis... and 30 U.S. Army soldiers...") is acceptable for takeouts/investigative pieces but not routine news stories, and should be discussed with an editor first; it must note when accounts could not be independently verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-rule definitions: on record, on background, deep background, off record
rubrics_metrics.description: On the record: quotation attributable to the source by name. On background / not for attribution: information attributable to a general, unnamed category (e.g., "a police department official"); reporters should push for maximum specificity. Deep background: information usable in the story but with no attribution at all — discouraged because readers get no way to judge where it came from. Off the record: information that cannot be used in the paper or in further reporting at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground rules must be established at the start of an interview (ideally on tape), not renegotiated retroactively — once a quote is on the record, it stays on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoted statements must be put in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements quoted must be put in context; potentially controversial statements by public figures should be quoted in a complete sentence or paragraph where possible, including what question was being answered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No pseudonyms; unnamed sources cannot attack by name-calling
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post does not publish ad hominem quotations from unnamed sources — sources wanting to attack someone must do so by name. Blind quotations added only for color should be avoided. No pseudonyms are used, and readers are never misled about identities; any decision to use less than a full name requires editor involvement and an explanation to readers of why.
